sections.title: Objective type questions: each has two parts of 1 mark.

questions.q: Define adolescence.
questions.answer: The period of transition from childhood to adulthood marked by physical and psychological changes and new social roles.

questions.q: Name any two secondary sexual characteristics of girls.
questions.answer: Rounding of hips, breast development, appearance of pubic hair, menstruation (any two).

questions.q: Name any two secondary sexual characteristics of boys.
questions.answer: Pubic hair, facial hair and change of voice (any two).

questions.q: What is a developmental task?
questions.answer: A problem that individuals typically face at a given period of life and must master.

questions.q: Who listed the developmental tasks of adolescence and how many?
questions.answer: Robert Havighurst listed ten tasks.

questions.q: Name the male and female sex hormones.
questions.answer: Testosterone in males; estrogen in females.

questions.q: State true or false: (i) The length of adolescence is mainly social. (ii) Gender consistency appears by age 3.
questions.answer: (i) True. (ii) False – at 6–7 years.

questions.q: Fill in: (i) The gland that controls adolescent growth is the ______. (ii) The primary sign of maturity in girls is ______.
questions.answer: (i) pituitary. (ii) menarche.

questions.q: What is gender identity?
questions.answer: A child's recognition, established by age 3–4, that they belong to one sex.

sections.title: Objective type questions: each has four parts of 1 mark.

questions.q: Give the factors of the pattern of adolescent transition: (i) the pace; (ii) the duration; (iii) the training; (iv) the status.
questions.answer: (i) Speed of transition. (ii) Length of transition. (iii) Discontinuities in training. (iv) Ambiguous status.

questions.q: Name the order in boys: (i) first change; (ii) second; (iii) third; (iv) final changes.
questions.answer: (i) Enlargement of testes. (ii) Pubic hair. (iii) Axillary hair. (iv) Voice change and beard.

questions.q: Name the order in girls: (i) first; (ii) second; (iii) third; (iv) fourth.
questions.answer: (i) Breast enlargement. (ii) Pubic hair. (iii) Menarche. (iv) Axillary hair.

questions.q: Match: (i) pituitary (ii) testosterone (iii) estrogen (iv) Erikson; with (a) female hormone (b) identity crisis (c) growth controller (d) male hormone.

sections.title: Very short answer questions. Answer in 30–50 words.

questions.q: Why is adolescence called a period of stress, strain and storm?
questions.answer: Rapid changes, ambiguity of role and conflicting demands bring conflicts, crises and dilemmas.

questions.q: What is meant by asynchronization of development?
questions.answer: Skeletal and muscular growth is faster than learning to use the new muscle mass, so the body needs new learning.

questions.q: Distinguish primary and secondary sex characteristics.
questions.answer: Primary are the reproductive organs (maturity shown by menarche or first ejaculation); secondary are observable features such as voice change and body hair.

questions.q: What is meant by gender role?
questions.answer: Society's expectations of how males and females should behave and the roles they should perform.

questions.q: How do advanced and simple cultures differ in giving adult status?
questions.answer: Advanced cultures give adult status at legal age; simple cultures require young people to show it through puberty rites.

questions.q: Why are girls' strength levels lower than boys'?
questions.answer: Biologically boys have broader shoulders, bigger chests and better leverage; culturally girls are encouraged to be weak and dependent.

questions.q: What is the identity crisis according to Erikson?
questions.answer: Failing to integrate various roles into a consistent self-identity causes confusion about who one is.

sections.title: Short answer questions. Answer in 50–80 words.

questions.q: Why is adolescence both biological and social?
questions.answer: It begins with biological changes of puberty and secondary sex characteristics, but its length depends on social factors such as leaving home, getting a job and voting; western and eastern adolescents differ owing to social norms.

questions.q: Explain any three factors that determine the pattern of transition.
questions.answer: Speed of transition: very fast changes with little preparation; length: early maturers are expected to behave like adults, prolonged adolescence fosters dependency; discontinuities in training: trained to be submissive yet now asked to be responsible.

questions.q: List the developmental tasks of adolescence (any six).
questions.answer: Mature relations with age mates; masculine or feminine role; accepting one's physique; emotional independence; economic independence; choosing an occupation; preparing for marriage; civic skills; responsible behaviour; values and ethics.

questions.q: Describe the growth spurt in adolescence.
questions.answer: Girls at 10–11 and boys at 12–13 show rapid height and weight growth for 3–4 years, linked to the pituitary gland; peak at 12.6 years in girls and 14.8 in boys; a child may grow 6–8 inches and gain 18–22 kg in a year.

questions.q: Explain the development of strength and skill in adolescent boys and girls.
questions.answer: Androgens, broader shoulders, bigger chest, lungs and heart give boys more strength, agility and coordination; girls' strength rises more slowly because of biological differences and cultural encouragement to be weak.

questions.q: Distinguish gender identity and gender consistency.
questions.answer: Gender identity, known by age 3–4, is awareness of being a boy or girl though children are unsure it is permanent; gender consistency, by 6–7 years, is the understanding that sex stays the same despite clothes or behaviour.

sections.title: Long answer questions. Answer in 80–120 words.

questions.q: Explain the physical development and sexual maturation in adolescence.
questions.answer: Pubescence brings a growth spurt controlled by the pituitary gland (girls 10–11, boys 12–13, peak 12.6 and 14.8 years). Asynchronization occurs as bones and muscles outgrow skills; proportions change. Sex hormones (testosterone, estrogen) cause primary and secondary sex characteristics in a fixed sequence; boys gain more strength.

questions.q: Describe the developmental tasks of adolescence given by Havighurst.
questions.answer: He listed ten tasks: mature relations with age mates, gender role, accepting physique, emotional independence, economic independence, occupation, marriage and family life, civic competence, social responsibility, and a value system. Success leads to success later; failure leads to unhappiness. Cultures differ in giving adult status.

questions.q: Discuss the major challenges and factors affecting the transition of adolescence.
questions.answer: Adolescence is a period of stress and storm with identity confusion. Factors: speed and length of transition, discontinuities in training, dependency, ambiguous status, conflicting demands, degree of realism and motivation. Delinquency, addiction and suicide may rise; removing barriers raises motivation.

questions.q: What is adolescence? Discuss whether it is biological or social and the role of gender roles.
questions.answer: Adolescence is the transition from childhood to adulthood. Biologically it starts with puberty and secondary sex characteristics; socially its length depends on independence markers and cultural norms. Gender roles are society's expectations for males and females; gender identity develops by 3–4 years and consistency at 6–7.
